entry.title: GitHub Actions: A Successful Job Is Not Publication Evidence
entry.summary: A scheduled publishing job can finish successfully without creating a public post. That is not necessarily a defect. The job might have selected the other daylight-saving trigger, found no reviewed content, performed a dry run, or recognised a publication that already exists. The mistake is treating every successful workflow conclusion as the same business outcome. A useful publisher records what happened to the publication attempt, then keeps that evidence separate from the health of the surrounding job. A workflow conclusion answers whether its steps met the runner's success conditions. It does not establish that a provider accepted a post, made it public, or returned the destination you expected. entry.title: Sustained Focus Depends on Returning, Not Perfection
entry.summary: Maintaining focus is often treated as a test of willpower: keep your eyes on the task and refuse every interruption. That standard sounds admirable, but it confuses uninterrupted attention with sustained progress. Real work includes small disruptions—a question from a colleague, a file that needs locating, a thought about an errand. The useful question is not whether attention ever moves. It is how reliably you can return. Imagine drafting a report at a shared desk. You reach a difficult paragraph, pause to check one source, answer a quick question, then come back to a blinking cursor. If you judge the session only by its interruptions, it looks like failure. Yet the report may be moving forward. Conversely, sitting still for an hour while rereading the same sentence can look focused without producing much. Before stepping away, leave a short breadcrumb: the question you were answering, the next action, or the sentence you planned to test. It need not become a tracking system. A note such as “compare these two examples, then write the contrast” can spare you from reconstructing the whole mental route when you return. For difficult work, I would protect the first stretch from optional interruptions, then judge the session by how often I regained the thread and what I advanced. Someone doing careful analysis may need longer quiet; someone coordinating a team may need a more flexible rhythm. Neither case proves that focus must be either perfect or absent. What helps you resume after an interruption without losing the shape of the task? https://apps.apple.com/se/app/focus-timer-desk-clock/id6762793543?l=en-GB Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.focus.timer.desk.clock
